title: Translation and style
intro: Translating Turkish is mostly a matter of order, and of what English has to add or leave out. One Turkish word can hold a whole English clause; a Turkish sentence builds everything before its last verb; `-mIş` and `-DIr` carry an attitude that English has to spell out in words; and some Turkish words and formulas have no English twin at all. This last unit of the course gathers the moves translators make, in both directions, and the questions to ask about a text's style before you start.

sections.title: Unpacking long words and left-branching sentences

blocks.text: **Read a long word from its root, and translate it from its end.** A suffix chain adds meaning from the inside out, and English usually says the same things in the opposite order. The folk tongue twister *Çekoslovakyalılaştıramadıklarımızdan mısınız?* is the famous extreme; built up one suffix at a time, it is ordinary grammar.

blocks.caption: One word, built up
head: Turkish
English
rows: to be unable to make (someone) Czechoslovak
the ones we couldn't make Czechoslovak
Are you one of the ones we couldn't make Czechoslovak?

blocks.text: Look at the last line. English starts with what Turkish puts last, the question and the person (*mısınız*, **are you**), then the case (*-dan*, **one of**), then the owner (*-ımız*, **we**), and only then the verb and its root. In practice, find the end of the word, or of the sentence, first.

**Left-branching sentences.** In Turkish everything that describes a noun comes before it, and everything that depends on a verb comes before the verb ([B1 unit 5](gp-relative-order)). English puts relative clauses after their noun and objects after their verb. So a translator reads a long Turkish sentence from the end: the main verb (*yüklem*), then its subject, then the noun phrases, turning each participle into a relative clause.

blocks.caption: *Annemin dün akşam bize anlattığı, dedemin gençliğinde İstanbul'da oturduğu ev artık yok.*
head: Step
Turkish
English
rows: the house is no longer there
2. The participle next to the noun
the house in Istanbul where my grandfather lived as a young man
annemin dün akşam bize anlattığı ev
the house my mother told us about last night

blocks.text: Put together: **The house in Istanbul where my grandfather lived as a young man, which my mother told us about last night, is no longer there.** That is correct, but heavy. English readers are happier with two sentences: **Last night my mother told us about the house in Istanbul where my grandfather lived as a young man. It is no longer there.** Splitting a long Turkish sentence is not a betrayal; it is often the faithful choice.

**And back into Turkish.** Going the other way, move every English relative clause in front of its noun as a participle ([B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik)): **the book that I lent you** → *sana ödünç verdiğim kitap*; **the woman who called** → *arayan kadın*. A **that** clause after a verb of saying or knowing becomes a noun clause ([B2 unit 4](gp-dik-clauses)): **She said that she was tired** → *Yorgun olduğunu söyledi*. And a verbal noun used as a subject is often best as a clause in English: *Gelmeniz önemli* → **It's important that you come**.

items.tr: Sana ödünç verdiğim kitabı okudun mu?
items.seg: Sana ödünç ver|diğ|im kitab|ı oku|du|n mu?
items.en: Have you read the book I lent you?
The woman who called yesterday called again.
Everyone was annoyed that Ali came late.
items.note: *Ali's coming late annoyed everyone* is correct but stiff.

items.tr: Annem dün akşam bize, dedemin gençliğinde İstanbul'da oturduğu evi anlattı.
items.seg: Anne|m dün akşam biz|e, dede|m|in genç|liğ|i|n|de İstanbul'|da otur|duğ|u ev|i anlat|tı.
items.en: Last night my mother told us about the house in Istanbul where my grandfather lived as a young man.

blocks.text: Don't keep the Turkish order in English, and don't turn every verbal noun into an English noun. *Gelmeniz bizim için önemli* is **It's important to us that you come**, rather than **Your coming is important for us**.

When a Turkish sentence runs to forty words, make two English sentences of it. When an English sentence has three relative clauses, a Turkish translator may turn one of them into a main clause of its own.

sections.title: -mIş, -DIr and the pronoun Turkish leaves out

blocks.text: English has no evidential suffix, so `-mIş` ([B1 unit 3](gp-evidential-mis)) has to be translated by the job it does. Ask which of four things it is doing: passing on what someone said, drawing a conclusion from evidence, registering a surprise or a discovery, or telling a tale.

blocks.caption: One suffix, many Englishes
head: Turkish
Situation
English
rows: Ali's here, apparently. / I hear Ali has arrived.
you see his coat in the hall
Ali must be here! / Looks like Ali's here!
you see a child after a year
It turned out the door was open.
He had something very important to do, supposedly!

blocks.text: English has a whole kit for these jobs: **apparently**, **reportedly**, **it seems**, **I hear**, **they say**, **must have**, **it turned out** ([C1 unit 7](gp-meger)), and for surprise the present perfect with an exclamation. Use the kit once per passage, not once per verb. Turkish repeats `-mIş` on every verb of a story; English says **apparently** once, or **according to my neighbour**, and then goes on in the plain past.

**`-DIr` works differently.** As an assumption ([C1 unit 2](gp-dir-assumption)) it means **must** or **probably**: *Yorulmuştur* is **She must be tired**. In formal and encyclopedic style ([B2 unit 5](gp-dir-formal)) it adds no doubt at all, and English simply states: *Müze pazartesi günleri kapalıdır* is **The museum is closed on Mondays**, and *Roman 1900'de yayımlanmıştır* is **The novel was published in 1900**. News Turkish, which avoids `-mIş` ([C2 unit 1](gp-news-reporting)), marks distance with verbs instead: *iddia edildi* is **allegedly** or **it was claimed**.

**The pronoun Turkish leaves out.** Turkish drops subject pronouns, and *o* is **he**, **she** and **it** at once. English must choose. Look back in the text for the person; if the text never says, as in a riddle or a story that keeps it open on purpose, English can use **they** or rephrase. The possessive is just as open: *Annesini aradı* is **he called his mother**, **she called her mother** or **they called their mother**. In the other direction, an English **she** vanishes into a verb ending; when the genders matter, Turkish names the people: *kadın*, *adam*, *kız*. And *sen* and *siz* both become **you**, so a translator into English shows the register in other ways: a first name, **sir**, a more formal tone.

items.en: It turned out nobody had locked the door.
They must have arrived long ago by now.
She came in, sat down and said nothing.
items.note: Or **he**: only the text before can tell.
Turkish names the people where English uses gendered pronouns.

blocks.text: French has a reportative of its own, the conditional of the press: **Le ministre aurait démissionné** is close to *Bakan istifa etmiş*. Both pass the news on without vouching for it; English needs **reportedly** or **is said to have**.
Don't translate every `-mIş` as **apparently**. In a tale it is simply the past, and three *apparently*s in a row sound like sarcasm.

sections.title: Reading style: length, origin, register, rhythm

blocks.text: Before translating a text, or answering a question about its tone, look at four things. Each one is easy to see once you know where to look.

blocks.caption: Four questions about style
head: Feature
What to look for
What it usually signals
rows: short main clauses (*Gitti. Dönmedi.*), or long chains of `-(y)Ip`, `-(y)ArAk` and participles
speed, tension, speech; or description, argument, officialdom
Arabic and Persian (*mesele, hürriyet, binaenaleyh*), reform words (*sorun, özgürlük, yanıt*), Western loans (*problem, organize etmek*)
age and solemnity; a modern written tone; everyday city talk ([C2 unit 3](gp-ottoman-pairs))
official or academic writing; or casual speech ([C1 unit 8](gp-spoken-vs-written))
words after the verb, repetition, pairs such as *eş dost*, sound patterns

blocks.text: **One piece of news, four styles.** The same fact can be written in very different Turkish, and each version needs a different English.

items.en: It has been decided to postpone the meeting.
items.note: Official: a passive, a verbal noun, `-mIştIr`.

items.en: Meeting postponed. / The meeting has been postponed.
The meeting's been put off, just so you know.
Postponed, the meeting. Nobody was surprised.
items.note: Literary: the verb first, then a short sentence.

blocks.text: **Keep the level when you translate.** Formal Turkish goes into formal English (**It has been decided…**, **Visitors are kindly requested…**), not into a word-for-word passive; casual Turkish into casual English; and an Ottoman word used for effect into an old-fashioned or mock-solemn English word, or into a tone. A translation that is correct but in the wrong register is still a mistranslation.

**Word origin is a choice.** Turkish writers choose between near-synonyms of different origin: *sorun, mesele, problem*; *yanıt, cevap*; *olanak, imkân*. The reform word often sounds modern and written, the older one traditional or simply everyday, the Western one urban and casual. When you write Turkish, match the text: an academic article takes *sorun* and *olanak*, a chat with a neighbour *problem* and *imkân*.

Count before you judge: underline the finite verbs of a paragraph. A paragraph with two finite verbs and ten participles is written Turkish, whatever its subject; one with ten short finite verbs is speech or a story told fast.
`-mAktAdIr` is not **is being** each time it appears. On a notice, *Çalışmalar devam etmektedir* is **Work is in progress** or **Work continues**.

sections.title: Words that don't travel: hüzün, gurbet, kolay gelsin

blocks.text: Some Turkish words and formulas have no English twin. Translators then have four tools: keep the word and explain it once; use a functional equivalent, the thing an English speaker would say in the same situation; explain it in a phrase; or leave it out where English would say nothing.

blocks.caption: Six hard cases
head: Turkish
Literally
In English, depending on the situation
rows: melancholy, wistfulness; in literary translation often kept as *hüzün*
living away from home, abroad; *gurbetçi*, a Turkish emigrant worker, especially in Western Europe
nothing, or **Hope it's going well**, **Don't work too hard**
**I'm not in the mood** (*keyfim yok*), **Enjoy it** (*keyfini çıkar*), **As you like** (*keyfin bilir*)
**the evil eye**; *Nazar değmesin!* after a compliment, much like **touch wood**
**Congratulations**, **All the best with it**, **Good luck in the new place**

blocks.text: **Hüzün.** TDK explains *hüzün* with words for grief and sorrow, but in use it is softer and often shared: a melancholy that can be almost beautiful ([C2 unit 2](gp-literary-forms) met it among the literary words). Orhan Pamuk's memoir *İstanbul: Hatıralar ve Şehir* (2003) made it known abroad as the collective melancholy of a city, and its English translation keeps the word *hüzün* as the title of a chapter.

**Gurbet** is being far from home, in another country or another city; *gurbete çıkmak* is to leave home to work elsewhere. **Exile** is too strong and **abroad** too flat. Folk songs of *gurbet* are a genre of their own, and since the 1960s *gurbetçi* has meant the Turkish workers who went to Western Europe, and often their families.

**Formulas** are the hardest, because English says nothing at those moments. *Kolay gelsin* to a shop assistant, *Hayırlı olsun* for a new car, *Geçmiş olsun* to someone with a cold ([A2 unit 7](gp-set-wishes)): in subtitles and dialogue, translators write what an English speaker would really say, or nothing. In a novel they may keep the formula and let the scene explain it.

items.en: I'm not in the mood at all this evening.
items.note: *Keyif* loses its i before a vowel: *keyfim*, *keyfini*.

items.en: My brother has been living away from home for years.
What a lovely child, touch wood!

blocks.text: People pin a blue *nazar boncuğu* on babies, doors and cars ([A1 unit 2 interlude](a1-u02-culture)), and many add *Nazar değmesin* to a compliment, much as English speakers touch wood or knock on wood.
Don't over-explain. A subtitle that turns *Kolay gelsin* into **May your work come easy to you** makes a two-second greeting sound like poetry.

summary: Read long words and sentences from the end: the last suffix or the main verb usually comes first in English.
Turn participles into relative clauses and verbal nouns into clauses, and split long sentences when English would; into Turkish, move relative clauses in front of their noun.
`-mIş` has no English twin: use **apparently**, **must have**, **it turned out**, a surprised present perfect, or the plain past of a tale, once per passage rather than once per verb.
`-DIr` is **must** or **probably** as an assumption, and nothing at all in a formal statement.
Turkish drops pronouns and *o* has no gender: English must choose **he**, **she**, **it** or **they**; Turkish names the people when gender matters.
Style lives in sentence length, word origin, register and rhythm; keep the level when you translate.
For *hüzün*, *gurbet*, *keyif* and formulas like *Kolay gelsin*: keep and explain, find a functional equivalent, explain in a phrase, or say nothing.
